PASTE ME. Click anywhere below the line, then Ctrl-A, Ctrl-C, and paste into the Substack editor. Everything above the line is scaffolding and is excluded from the selection. If figures do not come through on the first paste, undo and paste a second time — that is the known behaviour, not a failure. Fallback: substack/assets/ holds every image numbered in paste order.

Ten areas in the western United States where one specific, measurable piece of crustal physics is most strongly expressed — a recently ruptured extensional fault cutting quartz-rich crystalline rock. Found by screening every normal fault the United States Geological Survey has mapped in the lower forty-eight, with every piece of folklore held out of the arithmetic. Two rounds of work, seventeen measured legs, both declared controls landing on their declared answers. If you were going to take instruments into the field and look for anomalous lights, this is where we would send you.

The observation this starts from

There is an observation in the anomalous literature old enough and repeated enough that almost everyone working in the field has some version of it: the reports are not spread evenly over the ground. They cluster. Jacques Vallée called the clusters window areas. Others have called them flap zones, hot spots, thin places, thresholds. The names differ; the observation is the same one, and it has survived seventy years of people noticing it.

What has not survived is any agreed explanation of why. The candidate answers divide roughly into three:

  • The clusters are about people. Reports pile up where observers pile up — near roads, towns, airbases, tourist overlooks — and the map of sightings is a map of witnesses with a light dusting of anything else.
  • The clusters are about culture. A place acquires a reputation, the reputation recruits reports, and the reputation is self-feeding. The record thickens where the record is already thick.
  • The clusters are about the ground. Something physical is different where the reports concentrate — the rock, the stress, the water, the field — and that difference either produces light and sound directly or makes a place unusually permeable to whatever else is going on.

Only the third makes a prediction you can go and check with instruments that nobody in this field controls. It is also the only one of the three that can tell you where to go rather than where people have already been. That is what this project set out to do, and what the list at the end of this report is.

The order of operations matters and it is the whole design. We did not start from the places with the reputations and look for physics underneath them. We started from the physics, screened the entire country on it blind, and only afterwards went and read what people say about the ground the screen picked out. The ten areas below are a prediction about where the mechanism should express itself, not a summary of where it has already been reported.

What we were looking for

We picked the most specific physical version of the third answer we could state, because a specific claim can fail and a vague one cannot.

The conjecture under test. Certain places host an anomalous light and sound record because of what the rock does there — specifically, that an extensional fault which has ruptured recently, cutting quartz-rich crystalline rock, supplies two things at once: a permeability pathway that opens rather than closes, and a source volume in which stress can be converted to charge.

The two halves matter separately.

Dilatancy. Faults are not all alike in what they do to the space around them. A thrust fault, under compression, closes porosity; the rock volume shrinks and fluid is squeezed out. A normal fault, under extension, does the opposite — it opens fracture space, and the fracture space becomes a route for fluid and gas from depth. If your mechanism needs anything to come up, you want an extensional structure, and you can tell which is which from the mapped slip sense without ever visiting.

Piezoelectricity, and one non-obvious consequence. Quartz converts mechanical stress into charge. It is the reason a quartz crystal keeps time and the reason a piezoelectric igniter throws a spark. Rock that is rich in quartz and under changing stress is, in principle, a source volume. But the obvious candidate is wrong, and this is the one place where the design departs from intuition: granite is a poor bet and a tectonic fabric is a good one. An equigranular pluton — an ordinary granite — has its quartz crystal axes pointing in every direction, so the individual moments average toward zero across any volume large enough to matter. A rock with a fabric — gneiss, schist, quartzite, mylonite — has been deformed, and deformation aligns the axes. Alignment is what lets small effects add up instead of cancelling. So the screen weights fabric above pluton, deliberately, against the folk expectation that granite is the magic rock.

Put the two halves together and you get a geographic prediction that is entirely independent of where anyone has ever seen anything: find every place in the country where a recently active extensional fault cuts quartz-rich crystalline rock, and the anomalous record should be heavier there than at matched places where it does not.

That is a claim that can lose. It is the reason the project exists in this shape.

The one decision that makes it a test

Here is the decision that turns the screen from a story into a test, and it cost a day of work to make.

The score contains no lore. No sighting count. No light record. No proximity to any facility, base, laboratory or reported incident. Nothing about what anybody has ever reported at any of these places entered the arithmetic that chose them.

An earlier survey of ours did the opposite, and it is worth saying exactly how it failed. It demoted a New Mexico fault for lacking a light record. That sounds reasonable and it is fatal: it ranks a site on the very thing the mechanism is supposed to predict. Every winner then carries lights, because carrying lights is what wins. The prediction cannot fail, so it is not a prediction. You have built a machine that congratulates you.

Holding the folklore out means the ten areas below were selected by rock, rupture age, slip rate, fault geometry and mapped structural scale — and then the folklore was looked up afterwards, at every site, including the ones where we expected nothing.

That is what buys the list its standing. Every one of these areas is on it because of what the rock does there. Not one of them is on it because someone saw something.

How the screen was built

The screen ran in six stages. Every stage is a script in the repository, every script writes its result to a JSON file, and every figure records the URL it pulled each layer from. Nothing below is a recollection; it is all re-runnable.

1 · The population. A complete national pull of the USGS Quaternary Faults and Folds database, layer 21 — 110,356 mapped sections, of which 53,301 carry a normal (extensional) slip sense. No sampling, no region of interest, no starting from anywhere in particular. Because a single long fault appears in the database as many separate mapped segments, the features were thinned to 1,399 nodes at least 40 km apart, so that one structure could not flood the list with copies of itself.

2 · The gate. For each of those 1,399 nodes, the geologic map lithology was sampled along the fault trace — eight vertices spread across the whole mapped extent of that fault system, not one point. A node passes if at least a quarter of its sampled vertices land in quartz-rich crystalline rock. All 1,399 were measured. Zero errors. 242 passed.

The along-trace detail is not fussiness. An earlier version of this probe sampled a single point, and it failed the one site we already knew the answer for — because the point landed 1.5 km off the trace in valley fill. A probe that samples where the fault is not will report that the fault is not there.

3 · The scoring legs. Survivors of the gate were scored on four further measured quantities, all from institutional sources, none of them about people:

  • Rupture age — how recently the fault has moved, from the Qfaults age class. A conduit that last opened in the Pliocene is not a conduit.
  • Slip rate — the mapped long-term rate, as a class.
  • Junction density — how many distinct extensional systems have mapped trace within 15 km. Intersections are where fracture networks connect.
  • Structural scale — total mapped length of the system.

A fifth leg, GPS strain from the MIDAS velocity field, was allowed to promote a site and never to demote one, because a missing GPS station is a fact about the geodetic network and not a fact about the fault. It reaches only 1.5% of the population and it annotates rather than decides.

Of the 242 gate survivors, 225 carry all four scoring legs and 17 carry some of them. Ranking is tiered on completeness first, so a fault measured on two legs cannot outrank a fault measured on four by holding a better average over fewer numbers.

4 · The composite. The four scoring legs plus the gate reading itself — the quartz fraction, which is a degree as well as a threshold — are averaged as five equal terms. That composite is what orders the list. One vertex of the eight sampled along a fault trace is worth 0.025 of it, and that step is the ruler this report measures its own distinctions against.

5 · From faults to areas. The deliverable is ten areas, not ten faults, and that is the coarser and more honest object. Without a separation rule the list is not a list of places, it is a list of one place said several times: four of the highest-scoring faults in the country sit inside a 13.7 km circle around Hebgen Lake. So the surviving structures were clustered by single linkage at 50 km — the frozen list's own separation scale — giving thirteen areas, each scored by its best-scoring member, and the top ten are printed. An area is a region of ground you could plan a field season around, and its members are named so nothing is hidden inside the cluster.

6 · The plates. Each area got a four-panel geophysical plate, built by the same code at every site so the eye can compare them: A shaded relief with Quaternary fault traces coloured by rupture age · B bedrock geology · C Bouguer gravity anomaly · D regional context with instrumental seismicity since 1900. Every layer in every panel records the request URL it came from, and no panel in any of the ten plates failed to load.

How it was controlled

This is the section that carries the machinery. Everything the reader needs in order to weigh the list is here, stated once. The rest of the report is the findings, and it does not stop to relitigate itself.

Controls declared before the run, not after

Two faults were named in writing before the national gate ran, with their required answers attached:

  • Sandia fault — declared POSITIVE. Must pass. It is where the project started; if the instrument cannot find it, the instrument is broken.
  • Hubbell Spring fault — declared NEGATIVE. Must fail. It is 19 km away in the same basin, and its trace runs in fan gravel.

Both came back exactly as declared: Sandia 0.875, pass. Hubbell Spring 0.000, fail. Two sites 19 km apart in the same basin, separated correctly, on answers written down before the run. That is the validated core of this programme and everything downstream stands on it.

A control whose right and wrong answers coincide measures nothing

Midway through, an obvious optimisation appeared: source the fault geometry from the local national pull instead of asking the server for each fault. Faster, same data. Run against the controls, the negative control agreed down both paths — 0.000 either way — and would have waved the change through on its own. The positive control disagreed: 0.875 declared against 1.000 by the shortcut.

The local file concatenates a fault's segments in a different order, and the probe samples every n-th vertex, so a different order means a different eight vertices. The change was rejected, and the incident produced the number that sets this report's resolution: the gate quantity carries roughly ±0.125 of sampling noise from vertex ordering alone — one vertex in eight. That is why no distinction below one vertex is asserted anywhere in this report, and why the ordering claims made further down are the specific ones they are rather than a ranking of all ten.

Three values, never two

The tempting query is show me the sites that meet all the requirements. Run naively it returns about twenty-one sites — and silently counts 1,376 unmeasured faults as failures. A short list looks like a strict screen. It is the same defect as a phantom zero, at population scale, and it is invisible in the output.

Standing rule adopted, and applied to every leg: a leg may only exclude a fault it actually measured. Every fault carries PASS / FAIL / UNMEASURED — three values, never two.

Why the gate reading is also a scoring term

The four scoring legs were run against the declared controls on their own, and they get the answer wrong: scored on age, slip, junctions and scale alone, Hubbell Spring — the declared negative — outscores Sandia by 0.19. That is the correct order reversed, on the only two sites whose answers were known in advance. Junction density is part of why: it reads 1.00 for both controls, saturated, carrying no information while passing every check that asks whether it is working.

So the composite this report ranks on does not use those four legs alone. The gate quantity — the fraction of sampled trace in quartz-rich crystalline rock — enters as a fifth equal term, because it is a degree and not only a threshold, and because it is the one leg with demonstrated discriminating power. Under the five-term composite the controls come out in the right order: Sandia 0.6108, Hubbell Spring 0.5874.

The margin is 0.0234 — about one vertex. Correctly signed, and small. That is the honest strength of the ordering, and it is why the list is read the way the next section describes rather than as a league table.

What the composite can order, and what it cannot

The ranking was tested against itself rather than assumed. Perturb the composite by one sampled vertex — 0.025, the smallest step the instrument takes — and ask which positions hold. The answer is specific and it sets how the list should be read:

  • Position 1 is resolved. Hebgen Lake holds first place under every perturbation. It is the only integer position in the study that does.
  • A head of four — Hebgen Lake, the Sierra front, the Carson Range, Centennial Valley — appears in the top ten in every draw. Their internal order does not resolve, and is not asserted.
  • The remaining six are on the list on merit and the composite cannot order them against each other. They are printed in score order because a list needs an order, and that order should not be read as a ranking.

The same ruler applies at the bottom edge. The gap between the tenth area and the eleventh is 0.0044 — about a fifth of one vertex. The tenth line therefore runs through the middle of a band rather than between two tiers, so the three areas immediately below it are printed by name alongside the ten instead of being cut silently.

The external test: this is a prediction, not a retrodiction

The screen's founding criterion was put to a test it could fail, against six anomalous locales this project did not choose and does not control — Marfa, Toppenish Ridge, Silver Cliff, the San Luis Valley, the Uinta Basin, Trout Lake — with 1,971 random western locations as the null.

The six famous locales are not sitting on recently ruptured normal faults. Their median distance to one is 30.2 km against the null's 20.1 km; none of the six is within 10 km of one, where 34.4% of random western ground is. The contrast is not statistically strong at n = 6 (p = 0.20), and its direction is the informative part.

That result is why this list is worth publishing. A screen that had come back agreeing with the famous locales would mostly have been rediscovering the map of where people already look. This one does not, which means the ten areas below are somewhere new — ground selected by a mechanism, not by a reputation. It also means the folklore in this report cannot be doing the work of evidence, and it is not asked to.

Pre-registration, matched decoys, and base rates predicted in advance

The three lore experiments were designed and committed to version control before any lookup ran. Frozen in advance: the tier ladder for each leg, the exact query strings, the readout threshold, the positive and negative controls, and the pairing rule. Each of the ten faults on the list as it stood when the experiments were frozen was matched to a decoy — a fault at least 100 km away, matched on observer density (census places within 50 km), scored under the identical rubric.

Three near-unity base rates were also predicted in advance: that some Indigenous material and some settler-history material would exist at essentially every site in the study, winner and decoy alike. Both landed at 20 out of 20. Those are not findings. They are what "the historical record saturates the mountain West" looks like when you measure it, and predicting them in advance is what stops them from being mistaken for a result later.

Then the scorer was blinded

Freezing the questions does not blind the reader. Every rubric and query string was frozen — and the person assigning tiers still knew which site was the winner and which was the decoy while reading the results, and tier assignment is a judgement call at every boundary: recurring or one-off, named or unnamed, place-specific or regional, whether 25.9 km counts as inside 25.

So it was run again properly. Labels stripped, all twenty sites shuffled into one list at a committed seed, nine independent scorers who could not see which site was which, two pre-declared probe items per leg gating each scorer's column, unblinding only at readout. Blinding moved every leg by a tenth of a tier or less, and it moved the winners down rather than up. The tier assignments in this report are the blind ones wherever the two differ, and both are printed at every site.

The confounds that are live, named once

Three, and they all bear on the anecdotal record at the end rather than on the physics that chose the sites:

  • Proximity to people. The screen's winners sit a median 7.5 km from a census place; their matched decoys 19.3 km. Any measure of how much has been written about a place is partly a measure of how many people have been standing in it.
  • The three lore legs are not independent. Rank correlation between them runs 0.32 to 0.48 across the twenty scored sites, and it survives replacing the scorer. They agree because of a property of the sites, so three weak agreements are worth closer to one.
  • Name salience. Winners carry famous names — Madison, Helena, Teton, Sandia. Several decoys are literally "unnamed fault near X". Five of twenty first-pass searches returned the wrong state entirely. This runs in the winners' favour and has not been removed.

Two instrument defects, found and fixed

The seismicity panel was reading a thirty-day window under a caption saying "all years". The USGS earthquake catalogue service defaults its start time to the last thirty days when the parameter is omitted; it does not warn, and it returns a small, honest-looking number. Re-run with an explicit 1900 start, the Sandia panel goes from zero events to 92, magnitude 1.6 to 4.7, with the Socorro cluster where it belongs. Every plate in this report carries the corrected window.

Then the fix hit a cap. With the window open, four sites returned exactly 20,000 events — the service's maximum record count, not a fault count, silently keeping the largest events and dropping the rest. Fixed by raising the magnitude floor per site until the returned count sits below the cap, and by printing both the requested floor and the plotted floor on every panel. A returned count equal to a round number probably names a cap.

What the screen found

The gate works. A complete national population, 1,399 nodes, 100% measured along-trace, zero errors, 242 passing, and both declared controls landing exactly on their declared answers — Sandia 0.875 and through, Hubbell Spring 0.000 and out. It discriminates: about one node in six passes, so it is not waving everything through. It has a stated noise floor. Anyone with an internet connection and the scripts can re-run it.

And it says something real about the country. The survivor population is dominated by intraplate crystalline-cored rift flanks and hotspot-flank terrain — the Rio Grande rift, the Yellowstone parabola, the eastern Sierra front, the Basin and Range margins. Those are the places where the continent is being pulled apart over old, deformed, quartz-bearing basement, which is precisely the conjunction the conjecture asks for. The criterion selects a coherent geological province, not a scatter. That is the first thing a screen like this has to do before anything it says about individual sites is worth reading, and it does it.

Thirteen areas emerge from the 242 at the 50 km scale. Ten are below.

How to read the list

Two things about the list's shape, so it is read for what it is.

Position one is a real result. Hebgen Lake holds first place under every perturbation the instrument can take. It is not a photo finish and it is not an artefact of where the cut fell: the Madison fault scores 0.8370 against 0.7324 for the next area, a gap of four vertices where most of the list is separated by less than one. If you can only go to one place, that is the place, and the screen says so unambiguously.

The membership is a floor, not a ceiling. 242 nodes passed the gate and ten areas are printed. The screen is telling you these ten are in the qualifying class and that the first is exceptional. It is not telling you the other 232 are empty — a site you care about may well be among them, and the whole ranked population is in the repository for anyone who wants to look their own ground up.

What is already written about this ground

The physics chose the sites. Then, and only then, we went and read what people say about them.

This section is anecdotal and it is offered as anecdote. It is not what puts any area on the list, and no area's position moves by a single vertex on anything in it. It is here because when you have predicted a piece of ground from first principles, it is worth knowing what is already written about that ground — and because the honest way to look is to look everywhere, including at the places you expect to come up empty.

So it was done as an experiment rather than a browse. Three legs, each with its own rubric, its own queries frozen in version control before any lookup ran, its own controls, and its own pre-declared bar of +1.0 tiers of separation between a site and its matched decoy — a fault at least 100 km away, matched on how many people live near it, read under the identical rubric.

  • H1 — anomalous light and sound record. Does the site carry reports of unexplained lights, hums, or related phenomena?
  • H2 — Indigenous place-narrative, anomaly-shaped. Not "were Native people here" — that is true everywhere and was predicted to be true everywhere. Specifically: is there a named locus at this place carrying spirit-being, power-place or transformation narrative?
  • H3 — US and settler historical record. Is there a place-specific, archivally attested settlement, mining or incident record?

H3 is the odd one out and it is in the design on purpose. It is the closest thing available to a control for human attention: settler history is dense where people went, and people went where the terrain, water and metal were. If the winners beat their decoys on H3 by about as much as on H1, then what the record is tracking is where people go.

All three legs, sighted and blind, against their pre-declared bar of +1.0 tiers.

Every leg leans toward the screen's sites, and pooled across all thirty comparisons 16 of 22 non-tied pairs favour the winner — a pooled separation of +0.63 tiers at p = 0.0525. Read blind, the separations are +0.7 on lights, +0.2 on Indigenous place-narrative, and +1.0 on settler history.

Against the +1.0 bar the pre-registration set, that is one leg at the line and two below it. As a test of the mechanism it does not carry, and we are not asking it to. As anecdote — as the answer to "what is already written about the ground the physics picked?" — it says the screen's areas are places with more attached to them than their matched comparisons, consistently, across three independently rubricked readings.

Two things sharpen what that is worth, and they cut in opposite directions.

The settler-history leg is the strongest one. That leg exists as the control for human attention, and it separating hardest is the signature of a record that tracks where people went. Consistent with that, the screen's areas sit a median 7.5 km from a census place against their decoys' 19.3 km. Restrict to pairs where both sit inside 25 km and the lights leg falls from +0.7 to +0.4. A good part of the anecdotal record is the geography of who was standing there.

And the part that is not. +0.4 is what survives that filter, on the lights leg, with distance neutralised. It is a small number on ten pairs and it is not a result. But it is the residue after the obvious deflation, it points the same way, and it is why the anecdote is worth printing next to the physics rather than instead of it.

Two areas — Centennial Valley and Antelope Valley — entered the deliverable in round two, after the lore experiments had been designed and run. They have no record entry below. Looking them up now, knowing they are on the list, is exactly the contamination the pre-registration exists to prevent, so they are printed with their ground and without their record. The blank is deliberate.

What this report claims

What this report claims. These are the ten areas in the lower forty-eight where a recently ruptured extensional fault cutting quartz-rich crystalline rock is most strongly expressed, measured from institutional records over a complete national population, with the anomalous record held out of the selection entirely. If the conjecture is right about what makes a place permeable, this is the ground it points at. This is where we would send an instrument.

The claim is about the physics, and the physics is measured. What remains open is the link between that physics and the phenomena — and that link is not something a desk study can close. It needs somebody on the ground with a magnetometer, a radon detector and a camera on a timer.

That is the point of publishing a list rather than an argument. An argument you can agree with. A list you can go and check.

The ten areas

Selected on rock, rupture age, slip rate, junction density and structural scale, every one of those measured from institutional records over a complete national population, before a single piece of folklore was looked up. Each area is a cluster of qualifying structures at 50 km, scored by its best-scoring member; extent is how far across the area runs and structures is how many qualifying faults it contains.

The ten areas, with the measured quantities that selected them.

And the three immediately below the cut

The gap between tenth and eleventh is 0.0044 — about a fifth of the smallest step this instrument takes. A cut that fine runs through the middle of a band rather than between two tiers, so the next three are printed by name instead of disappearing.

Printed rather than dropped: the three areas immediately under the tenth line.

What follows is the ten, each with its four-panel geophysical plate, its measurements as the screen took them, and — where it exists — what the record says about that ground.

How to read the plates. All four panels are built identically at every site. A shaded relief with Quaternary fault traces coloured by rupture age. B bedrock geology from the USGS state geologic map compilation, with the same linework. C Bouguer gravity anomaly — the density structure under the surface, where a steep gradient marks a basin edge. D regional context with instrumental seismicity since 1900. The star is the sampled node, on the fault trace.

How to read the tiers. Each leg scores 0 to 3 against a ladder frozen before any lookup ran. Written here as T for the light and sound leg, NT for the Indigenous place-narrative leg, HT for the settler historical leg — T0 means nothing qualifying was found, T3 means the strongest rung of that ladder. Every site is printed with its matched decoy: a fault at least 100 km away, matched on observer density, scored under the identical rubric. sighted is the original tier; blind is what the nine independent scorers assigned without knowing which site was which.

The evidence grades are uneven and the text says which is which. A federal register entry and a ghost-story aggregator both appear below, and they are not the same kind of thing. Where the record is thin the entry is short. Where an area has no record entry at all, it is one of the two that entered after the lore experiments were frozen.

#1 · Hebgen Lake, Montana

Hebgen Lake, Montana · 44.7920, -111.4380 · best-scoring structure Madison fault · score 0.8370 · gate reading 1.0 · nearest census place 19.7 km

Madison fault. A relief with Quaternary traces coloured by rupture age · B bedrock geology · C Bouguer gravity · D regional context with instrumental seismicity since 1900.

The ground

This is the only site in the ten whose fault ruptured in front of witnesses. On 17 August 1959 the Hebgen Lake earthquake — magnitude 7.5 — broke the ground here, dropped the lake basin, and brought eighty million tons of dolomite off the south wall of the Madison canyon in about a minute. Twenty-eight people died, most of them campers. The slide dammed the Madison River and the impoundment is still there, still full of standing dead timber, and it is still called Quake Lake.

The rock is the best in the study: 8 of 8 sampled vertices qualify, seven gneiss and one quartzite, along 305 km of mapped trace across 25 segments. That is a fabric rock, not a pluton — precisely the case the mechanism wants, where the crystal axes are aligned by deformation instead of pointing everywhere. Six distinct extensional systems have mapped trace within 15 km. The regional catalogue holds 25,016 events at magnitude 1 or above since 1900 within 90 km, which is among the most seismically active ground in the interior of the continent.

If the conjecture is right anywhere, the prior says it should be right here. Which is what makes the record below worth reading carefully.

    quartz_frac 1.0 = 8/8 vertices — 7× gneiss, 1× quartzite
    along 305.2 km of trace, 25 segments · gate cuts at 0.25 · sampling noise ±0.125 from vertex ordering
  • L2 · rupture age — PASS
    historic
  • L3 · slip rate — PASS
    Between 0.2 and 1.0 mm/yr
  • L4 · junction density — PASS
    6 dilatant systems within 15 km
    Hebgen fault; Madison fault; Red Canyon fault; West Fork fault; unnamed fault near Cliff Lake; unnamed fault near Mile Creek
  • L6 · structural scale — PASS
    98 km total mapped length
  • L5 · GPS strain (annotates only, may promote, never demotes) — UNMEASURED
    no GPS strain node within the layer's footprint; a statement about the network, not the fault

  • Instrumental seismicity (panel D) — PRESENT

The record

The anomalous record is empty. The frozen queries returned earthquake geology, in quantity, and one 2003 light report near West Yellowstone about 30 km out — a one-off, failing both clauses of the first rung of the ladder. Tier T0 sighted; T0 blind. The nine independent scorers, who did not know this was the top-ranked site in the country, agreed with the original zero.

Its matched decoy did better. Big Chino fault in Arizona, 16 km from Seligman, returned a town that appears repeatedly in FBI UFO files across the 1940s to 1960s with newspaper attestation — recurring, close, and archival. T2 sighted and blind. The number one site in the country was beaten on lights by its own control.

The Indigenous record is real and regional rather than local: this is ancestral Shoshone-Bannock country, described in the sources as long revered as sacred, but with no named locus on the range itself. NT1, and its decoy scored the same.

The settler record is the maximum: HT3 sighted and blind. The 1959 quake and the Madison Slide, twenty-eight dead, USGS and Association of State Dam Safety Officials sources; and before that Hebgen Dam, built 1914–15 by Montana Power. Its decoy scored HT1.

#2 · Sierra front / Walker Lane

Owens Valley above Bishop, California · 37.5420, -118.7260 · best-scoring structure Round Valley fault · score 0.7324 · gate reading 0.5 · nearest census place 2.4 km

Round Valley fault. A relief with Quaternary traces coloured by rupture age · B bedrock geology · C Bouguer gravity · D regional context with instrumental seismicity since 1900.

The ground

The eastern wall of the Sierra Nevada above Bishop, in the Owens Valley — one of the most actively extending places in North America and one of the deepest basins in the country relative to the range beside it. The Bouguer gravity across this plate spans 73 mGal, the largest range of the ten; that is the signature of a very deep sediment fill against a very dense range block.

The gate reading is mixed and honestly so: 4 of 8 vertices qualify, all four granite, the other four returning no qualifying unit, sampled along 771 km of trace across 156 segments. Granite is the weak version of the piezoelectric case, for the averaging reason set out earlier. What this site has instead is motion: latest-Quaternary rupture, a slip rate class of 1 to 5 mm/yr — the fastest bracket in the ten — seven distinct extensional systems within 15 km including the Long Valley caldera ring fault, and a GPS strain reading of 88.6 on a leg that reaches only 1.5% of the population at all.

The regional catalogue holds 175,460 events at magnitude 1 or above since 1900 within 90 km. That is not a typo and it is by far the highest in the study. Long Valley is a restless caldera.

Measured:

The record

The light record is regional and real but not local: the Eastern Sierra and Owens Valley carry a recurring sighting record, with Bishop in 2012 and Lone Pine in 1991 among the specific returns, all of it in the 25 to 60 km band rather than on the structure. T1 sighted and blind. Its decoy, the Thompson Valley fault in Montana, returned a single 2014 orb at a hot spring 28.5 km out — T0.

The Indigenous leg is where this site is instructive about the method rather than the mechanism. This is Payahuunadü, the land of flowing water, home of the Nüümü — and the strongest returns, the Volcanic Tableland petroglyph fields described in the sources as fragile and sacred, sit across the valley rather than on the fault. Under a rubric that requires a named locus at the place, that is NT1, and blind scorers dropped it to NT0.

Its decoy took that leg decisively. The Thompson Valley fault sits near a hot spring the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes call Big Medicine — a named power and healing place with centuries of documented ceremonial use, in tribal and Montana historic landscape sources. NT3 against the winner's NT1. The decoy did not merely match; it beat the winner by two full tiers on the leg that most directly asks whether the place itself is regarded as extraordinary.

The settler record is a tungsten mine in Inyo County, HT2. The nineteenth-century massacres in Mendocino County's Round Valley, several hundred kilometres away, were not credited to this site.

The Carson Range on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe. Small, sharp and busy: 17 km of mapped length — the shortest structure in the ten — but 11 distinct extensional systems within 15 km, the densest junction reading in the study by some margin, in a range front that is being pulled apart between the Sierra block and the Basin and Range.

The rock passes cleanly: 7 of 8 vertices granodiorite along 102 km of trace. The record

This site and Sandia are the two that score highest summed across all three legs, and it is worth being precise about what that does and does not mean.

Lights: the Lake Tahoe basin carries a recurring UFO record inside 25 km, in local press and in a regional folklore collection that files it as "Lost Legend #5". Recurring and close, but no named light — which caps it at T2, sighted and blind.

Indigenous place-narrative: the strongest in the study, and it is a real tradition rather than an internet artifact. This is Wašiw country — Dáʔaw, the lake — and Cave Rock, on the eastern shore, is a named locus in Washoe tradition associated with the Water Babies and with shamanic practice, attested in published folklore collections and in Forest Service tribal-history documentation. It is an actively protected sacred site. NT3 sighted and blind. It should be said clearly that this is a living tradition of a living people and not a curiosity; the rubric scored the density and specificity of the record, which is the only thing a rubric can do.

Settler history: HT3. The Hobart and Marlette sawmill operation ran in Little Valley itself from 1873, feeding timber to the Comstock; in 1884 a windstorm blew down a V-flume carried on an eighty-foot trestle and the crews rebuilt it in eight days. Little Valley Placers worked the ground. Truckee-Donner Historical Society sourcing.

Its decoy, the Bear River Range faults in Utah, scored T1 / NT2 / HT3 — including a 1949 light-and-explosion event in Sardine Canyon with FBI and newspaper attestation, which is better-sourced than anything on the winner's light leg but is a single event rather than a pattern. On the settler leg the decoy tied the winner at the ceiling.

#4 · Centennial Valley, Montana

the north wall of the Centennial Valley at Lakeview, Montana · 44.5840, -112.0660 · best-scoring structure Centennial fault · score 0.6812 · gate reading 0.5 · nearest census place 20.2 km

Centennial fault. A relief with Quaternary traces coloured by rupture age · B bedrock geology · C Bouguer gravity · D regional context with instrumental seismicity since 1900.

The ground

The north wall of the Centennial Valley in Montana, immediately west of Yellowstone — a seventy-kilometre east–west escarpment that is one of the few major east–west normal faults in a province where nearly everything else runs north–south. It sits at the west end of the Yellowstone hotspot parabola, where the crust that the hotspot has already passed under is still relaxing and pulling apart.

The gate reads 4 of 8 vertices qualifying — two gneiss, one quartzite, one schist — along 254.7 km of trace across 25 mapped segments, for a quartz fraction of 0.5. Every qualifying vertex is a fabric rock, so this site's fabric_frac equals its quartz fraction: the aligned-axis case the mechanism asks for, with none of it coming from equigranular pluton. A fifth vertex returned rhyolite, which is a measured rock at a measured point and does not count toward the gate; it is volcanic, and volcanic glass has no fabric to align.

Latest-Quaternary rupture, a slip rate class of 0.2 to 1.0 mm/yr, five distinct extensional systems within 15 km, and 62 km of total mapped length — behind only the Madison fault, and level with the Mosquito. The bedrock at the sampled node is quartzite of the Frontier Formation. The gravity field across the plate spans 29 mGal over 653 stations, a clean single basin edge: the valley floor is a downdropped block and the fault is its north bounding structure.

This area is a head-set member. It appears in the top ten in every perturbation of the composite, and it is the highest-scoring area in the ten that has never appeared in any published version of this list — it enters here because the deliverable moved from the 100 km separation scale to 50 km, and at 50 km the Centennial fault is its own area rather than a suburb of Hebgen Lake 54.8 km to the east.

#5 · Antelope Valley, California/Nevada

Antelope Valley at Topaz Lake, on the California–Nevada line · 38.6770, -119.5480 · best-scoring structure Antelope Valley fault zone · score 0.6244 · gate reading 0.25 · nearest census place 2.5 km

The ground

Antelope Valley at Topaz Lake, straddling the California–Nevada line at the northern end of the Walker Lane — the belt where the Sierra Nevada's eastern front hands its motion over to the Basin and Range, and where extension and strike-slip are braided together across a wide zone of distributed faulting.

The gate reading here is the lowest in the ten, level with the Sand Springs Range: 2 of 8 vertices qualifying, both granite, along 529 km of trace across 94 mapped segments, a quartz fraction of 0.25 sitting exactly on the gate's cut. Two further vertices returned rhyolite — measured, named, and not qualifying. The qualifying rock here is plutonic rather than fabric, which by this project's own reasoning is the weaker of the two cases.

What carries this area onto the list is geometry and motion. Seven distinct extensional systems within 15 km — behind only the Carson Range, and level with the Sierra front — across 51 km of mapped length, with latest-Quaternary rupture and a slip rate class of 0.2 to 1.0 mm/yr. Intersections are where fracture networks connect, and this is some of the most thoroughly intersected ground in the study. The plate's gravity field spans 47 mGal over 690 stations. The regional seismicity is dense enough that the magnitude floor had to be raised to 2.0 to keep the plotted catalogue inside the service's return cap; 9,762 events are drawn at that floor, and both the requested and plotted floors are printed on the panel.

Antelope Valley is also among the most accessible ground in the ten. The nearest census place is 2.5 km away and US-395 runs the length of the valley.

The ground

The fault runs along the north edge of the Helena valley, three kilometres from the suburbs of Montana's capital. The gate reading is one of only three perfect scores in the ten: 8 of 8 vertices quartzite, along 45 km of trace in just 8 mapped segments. Pure, uniform, quartz-rich metamorphic rock along the entire sampled length — and quartzite is a fabric rock, the version of the piezoelectric case the mechanism actually wants.

Against that, the motion is slow: late-Quaternary rather than latest, a slip rate class below 0.2 mm/yr, 20 km of mapped length. Five extensional systems within 15 km. The regional catalogue holds 5,894 events since 1900 within 90 km, plotted complete with no truncation.

This is the clearest example in the set of the tension the ranking cannot resolve: the best rock in the study attached to one of the slowest clocks.

The record

Lights: the region carries a genuinely named phenomenon — the Diamond City Light, in Confederate Gulch — but it sits about 60 km out, which under the frozen ladder puts it in the far band. T1 sighted and blind. A named, recurring light at 60 km scores lower than an anonymous one at 10 km, by rule, and the rule was written before anyone knew what was out there.

Indigenous place-narrative: NT2. About 16 km away, the Gates of the Mountains — the limestone canyon Lewis and Clark named in 1805 — holds some fifty pictograph sites with Blackfeet, Salish and Kootenai association and documented ceremonial use. The tier is capped at 2 rather than 3 partly because the first-pass sourcing came through listicle-grade aggregators as well as substantive ones, and the rubric penalises that.

Settler history: the maximum, and one of the densest records in the study. Last Chance Gulch — four Georgian prospectors, July 1864, on what they had agreed would be their last try before giving up. The camp was named Helena that October, became territorial capital in 1875, and produced on the order of three and a half billion dollars in gold in current terms. The gulch is now the main street. Montana Historical Society sourcing. HT3.

Its decoy is the site that most cleanly demonstrates the study's worst instrument defect. The Bull Mountain western border fault near Boulder, Montana, scored zero on all three legs — and the frozen queries returned the Bull Mountains coal field near Roundup, about 200 kilometres away, and Boulder County Colorado. Those zeros are name conflations, not absences. They are counted as zeros in the arithmetic anyway, because amending a query after seeing what it missed is how a null quietly becomes a positive.

The record

This site is the most valuable one in the report and it scored zero on everything.

T0, NT0, HT0, sighted and blind, all three legs. The light queries returned geology and one 2016 orb report logged at county level rather than site level. The Indigenous leg returned a travel corridor and hunting grounds and nothing anomaly-shaped — though it returned one lovely and entirely mundane fact, which is that Red Rock is named for beds of ochre used as paint. The settler leg conflated outright, returning Red Lodge in Carbon County about 350 km east and a Red Rock Mine in Fergus County, with nothing on-target at Dell.

Its decoy, the Lida faults in Nevada, beat it: an 1867 mining district, a town laid out in 1872, a post office and mill, a 1905 boom on the back of Goldfield that took the population to about three hundred and produced on the order of a million dollars. HT2, from ghost town aggregators and encyclopaedia entries — web-secondary sourcing, and graded as such.

Why is a site that scored nothing the most valuable one here? Because a screen that returns only places with stories is a screen that has been contaminated by its own hypothesis. This one returned a place with no stories, kept it on the list, and let it score zero three times. The null site is the evidence that the selection was honest. A screen where all ten came back loaded would not have been a screen that worked; it would have been a screen that was rigged.

The record

Lights: Fallon markets itself as the UFO Capital of the West and the record behind that is recurring rather than anecdotal — but the town sits 41 to 49 km from the sampled node, which lands it in the far band. T1, sighted and blind. Its decoy, the Lone Pine fault in Idaho, returned a recurring apparition near Clayton known since the 1920s as "Russian John" at 34 km, plus vague regional material. T1 as well. The lights leg is a tie.

Indigenous place-narrative: the strongest sourcing in the entire study, and the tier is NT3 sighted and blind on the back of federal documentation rather than folklore. Sand Mountain — a two-mile singing dune at the north end of the range — is a sacred site to the Fallon Paiute-Shoshone Tribe, with BLM management documents, Federal Register entries and congressional record behind that status. Nearby Spirit Cave held the oldest well-preserved human remains ever found in North America, repatriated to the tribe in 2016 after a twenty-year dispute; Grimes Point carries one of the densest petroglyph concentrations in the Great Basin.

Settler history: HT3 sighted, HT2 blind. The Sand Springs Pony Express Station was built here in 1859–60, abandoned in 1861 when the telegraph made it pointless, buried by the dunes for the better part of a century, and stabilised in 1997. And then there is the fact that outranks everything else on this plate for sheer strangeness of the record: on 26 October 1963 the United States detonated a twelve-kiloton nuclear device underground inside this range — Project SHOAL, a Vela Uniform experiment designed to measure how a nuclear explosion in granite looks to seismic instruments compared to an earthquake.

Sit with that for a moment against everything else in this report. The one site the screen picked where almost nobody lives is a site the federal government chose, for reasons entirely of its own, as a good place to see what happens when you shake crystalline rock very hard. Nothing follows from it. The screen did not know, and could not have known — but it is the kind of coincidence that this field is built out of, and the honest thing to do is print it and decline to build on it.

The ground

The Mosquito Range above Alma, Colorado, at the head of South Park — the highest incorporated town in the United States sits 7.6 km from this node, at 3,200 metres.

Another perfect gate reading: 8 of 8 vertices, six granite and two gneiss, along 254 km of trace. 62 km of mapped length, four extensional systems within 15 km, and the deepest Bouguer values in the study at −334 to −285 mGal, which is what a very thick, very high crustal root reads like.

And then the anomaly of the set: 95 catalogued earthquakes at magnitude 1 or above within 90 km since 1900. Ninety-five, against Round Valley's 175,460. This is nearly aseismic ground carrying nearly perfect rock, which is a combination the mechanism has no obvious use for — piezoelectric conversion needs stress to be changing. It is worth stating as an open tension rather than resolving it.

A reader who wants to discount it entirely is applying a stricter standard than ours, not a different one.

South Park is ancestral Ute — Nuche — hunting ground with roughly eight thousand years of documented use, and the queries returned nothing anomaly-shaped: no named locus, no power place, no transformation narrative at this location. That is a real zero for a real reason, and it is what a base rate that saturates on presence looks like when you ask a sharper question instead.

the west face of the Sandia Mountains, Albuquerque, New Mexico · 35.1530, -106.4720 · best-scoring structure Sandia fault · score 0.6108 · gate reading 0.875 · nearest census place 2.8 km

The ground

The west face of the Sandia Mountains, immediately above Albuquerque — and this is where the entire project started. It is on this list tenth, on the same arithmetic as everything above it, and that is the point: the founding site earned its place rather than being given one.

7 of 8 vertices granite along 327 km of trace across 56 segments, quartz fraction 0.875. This is the declared positive control for the whole national gate, and it passed. Its companion 19 km away, Hubbell Spring, is the declared negative control, and it failed at exactly 0.000. Both controls exact, which is the single most important result in this report.

Late-Quaternary rupture, slip below 0.2 mm/yr, five extensional systems within 15 km, 28 km of mapped length, a Bouguer range of 63 mGal across the plate — the Rio Grande rift basin edge is one of the sharpest density steps in the study. Only 92 catalogued events within 90 km since 1900.

That 92 has a history, told in the method section above: the first version of this panel reported zero events under a caption reading "all years", because the federal earthquake service silently defaults to a thirty-day window when you omit the start time. The panel then printed its own zero as a finding.

    along 327.4 km of trace, 56 segments · gate cuts at 0.25 · sampling noise ±0.125 from vertex ordering
  • L2 · rupture age — PASS
    late Quaternary
  • L3 · slip rate — PASS
    Less than 0.2 mm/yr
  • L4 · junction density — PASS
    5 dilatant systems within 15 km
    Faults north of Placitas; Rincon fault; San Felipe fault zone; San Francisco fault; Sandia fault
  • L6 · structural scale — PASS
    28 km total mapped length
  • L5 · GPS strain (annotates only, may promote, never demotes) — UNMEASURED
    no GPS strain node within the layer's footprint; a statement about the network, not the fault
  • Bouguer gravity (panel C) — PRESENT
    -231 to -168 mGal (range 63) from 710 stations in the padded box
  • Instrumental seismicity (panel D) — PRESENT
    92 catalogued events M≥1 since 1900 within 90 km; all 92 plotted, no truncation

The record

Lights: Albuquerque carries a recurring record inside 25 km, and the region's most famous entry — the Kirtland Air Force Base incident of 1957, in which control tower and radar personnel tracked an object over the base — is a named incident rather than a named recurring light, which the frozen ladder scores at the second rung — T2 — and not the top one. Blind scorers dropped it to T1. Its decoy, the Picuris-Pecos fault near Santa Fe, returned "Spook Lane" and the "Shades of Death Path" — named devil-light folklore, about 18 km out, on tour-operator sourcing — and also scored T2. The decoy tied the winner.

Indigenous place-narrative: NT3 sighted and blind. The Sandias are sacred to Sandia Pueblo; the Tiwa name for the range is Bien Mur, and the Pueblo holds an active sacred-sites claim with the Forest Service, in tribal and press sourcing. The decoy also scored NT3: Pecos Pueblo's kivas as places of communion with underworld spirits, plus "The Drowning of Pecos" from a printed folk-story collection predating 1995, National Park Service sourced. Tied again.

Settler history: this leg's declared positive control, and what happened to it is more useful than a clean pass would have been. It passed its declared condition and failed its declared content. The frozen query asked for settlement OR mining OR incident, and it duly returned the Montezuma silver boom of 1879–80 in Las Huertas Cañon with claims registered at the Albuquerque county seat, plus Sandia Man Cave and the Turquoise Trail workings. HT3. But the Sandia records this region is actually known for in the anomalous literature — Manzano, Kirtland, the Bennewitz affair — never appeared, because those are military and the frozen query has no clause for military. They were out of reach by construction.

The query was not amended mid-run. Amending a query after seeing what it missed is precisely how a null becomes a positive, and the discipline is worth more than the material would have been.

Where we would point an instrument

The list is a recommendation about where to point instruments, so here is what we would actually do with it.

Go to Hebgen Lake first. It is the only resolved position in the study, it outscores the second area by four times the instrument's own step, and it is the one site in the ten whose fault ruptured in front of witnesses — in 1959, magnitude 7.5, with the scarps still in the ground. Whatever the mechanism does, this is where it should be loudest.

What to carry. The conjecture makes physical predictions that a field party can test in a week, and they are cheap:

  • A magnetometer on a continuous log. Stress-driven charge separation in a quartz-bearing source volume should show as transient field excursions correlated with microseismicity, not as a steady anomaly. The correlation is the signal; the level is not.
  • Radon and soil gas along the trace. This is the direct test of the dilatant half of the conjecture — an extensional fault should be venting, and a thrust should not. Run the same instrument across a nearby compressional structure as your control.
  • Cameras on timers, at the scarp and off it. Matched pairs, same night, same weather. The whole point of a site list is that it lets you build a comparison instead of a collection.
  • Local seismic, at low magnitude. The catalogues used here are national and their completeness floors are coarse. The events the mechanism would care about are below them.

What would sharpen the screen itself. Two things, in order:

  • Aeromagnetic depth-to-basement. This is the correct version of the rock criterion wherever the crystalline source is buried rather than exposed. Surface geology cannot see it, and it would re-rank every basin-fill site in the study — including the one this project started from.
  • More labelled ground. Twenty to thirty sites with independently known answers would let the composite be trained rather than argued about. Right now it has two, and they are the two it was built around.

And two claims of our own that this work killed, recorded so nobody rebuilds on them: "the Sandia / Hubbell Spring junction ranks first in the continental US" — it ranks 36th of 242 — and an early geodetic result that had profiled the wrong velocity component. Both were ours. Both are withdrawn.

Why a list and not an argument

The map of anomalous reports is not a map of anomalous places. It is mostly a map of roads, towns and people with cameras, and everyone working in this field knows it. The only way out of that is to predict ground from something other than the reports — and then go and look.

That is what the ten areas are. They were chosen by rock, rupture age, slip rate, fault geometry and structural scale, over a complete national population, with the folklore held out of the arithmetic and the controls declared in writing before the run. The six most famous anomalous locales in the western United States are not on this list, and that is the strongest thing about it: the screen is not rediscovering where people already look. It is pointing somewhere else.

Everything here is re-runnable. The population, the gate, the scoring legs, the plates and their source URLs are all in the repository. If you think the weighting is wrong, change it and re-run it — the ranked list of all 242 survivors is there, and your ground may well be on it.

And if you get to one of these ten before we do, tell us what you found. Including nothing. Especially nothing.

Provenance and standing

Data. USGS Quaternary Faults and Folds (complete national layer-21 pull) · USGS State Geologic Map Compilation · Macrostrat geologic map lithology · USGS Bouguer gravity · USGS 3DEP shaded relief · ANSS / ComCat instrumental seismicity · MIDAS GPS velocity field · US Census place gazetteer. Every layer in every plate records the URL it was requested from.

Freezes. Each lore experiment's design, tier ladder and exact query strings were committed to version control before any lookup ran; the blind re-score design, packets and probe gate were committed before any scorer was dispatched. Commit hashes are in the repository record.

Checking. Every measurement quoted in this article is asserted at build time against the frozen artefact it came from — site measurements against the dossier and the stage-5 join, tiers against the lore result files, headline figures against the summaries, and the membership and order of the ten against candidate_list.json. A typo fails the build rather than shipping. The two areas added in round two were measured through the same along-trace probe as the other eight, with both declared controls run first and required to reproduce.

Standing. Screened, ranked, figured and written by Clawd, at Clayton's direction. The physics inputs are institutional and anyone may re-pull them; the weighting is ours. This has not yet been read by anyone outside this house.

Corrections, refutations and better instruments are all welcome, and the third is the most welcome.
